The display’s 250 nits brightness may be relatively modest, but we found that the E27u looks bright and sharp enough for working with productivity software such as Microsoft Office, and also for streaming video from the BBC iPlayer and Apple TV+. And while Apple charges an extra £400 for an upgrade that allows you to adjust the height of its Studio Display—which is more than the entire cost of the E27u—you can tilt, swivel and adjust the height of the E27u, and even rotate it into upright (portrait) mode at no extra cost.

The E27u includes HDMI, DisplayPort and USB-C interfaces for connecting to your Mac, with the USB-C port also providing 65W power to charge a MacBook or other laptop if required. When using the USB-C connection you can also use four USB-A ports to connect devices such a keyboard, mouse or hard drive, and there’s also a second DisplayPort interface that will allow you to daisy-chain a second monitor if required. Our only complaint is that there’s no audio connector that would allow you to connect headphones or a set of external speakers to the display – although HP does sell a special ‘speaker bar’ that bolts onto the bottom of the screen if you want to add audio ($43.00/£40.00).–Cliff Joseph

How we test monitors

Macworld staff and other contributors with decades of combined experience have tested the displays in this round up.

We thoroughly test each monitor, evaluating clarity of the image, maximum brightness, contrast ratio, and color accuracy and color gamut and other aspects of image quality. Motion clarity is also important, especially if the monitor will be used for gaming or other graphical applications.

We also look at the build quality as well as usability and connectivity, and any special features or modes on offer, especially any that require software that may, or may not work as expected on a Mac.

Why you should trust Macworld

Macworld prides itself on our experience and expertise when it comes to all things Mac. We conduct in-depth reviews of numerous monitors annually. Our comprehensive recommendations undergo rigorous testing and evaluation by our expert reviewers, who adhere to both performance benchmarks and stringent usability standards.

Should I buy an Apple display for my Mac?

Apple sells displays for its Macs, and you could go with its offerings, which are included above, but its displays are a quite bit more expensive than what third parties offer.

Buying from a different company may mean you may not get a feature that Apple offers, but it may also be a feature that you don’t need, depending on how you use the monitor.

There are plenty of companies that have great monitors that you can use with your Mac, without having to take out a second mortgage. Our sister publication PCWorld has tested several displays, and we list their top-rated ones that we have been able to confirm work with Macs, alongside the monitors we have reviewed below. Here are our recommendations in order, starting with Apple’s most expensive.

Are there compatibility issues for Mac monitors?

There are compatibility issues for plain M1, M2 and M3 Macs, which, unlike M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro/Max/Ultra MacBooks, can’t natively connect to more than one external display. Fortunately, there is a solution and we show you how to connect multiple monitors to M1, M2 and M3 Macs in a separate article.

How to choose a Mac monitor

Display technology is a bit of a movable feast, with a lot of confusing jargon and technical features to wade through, as well as a variety of different interfaces and cables that are used by Apple itself and the various monitor manufacturers. So it’s worth taking a closer look at some of the factors that you need to think about when buying a monitor for your Mac.

Screen size

Size isn’t everything, as the saying goes, but it’s a good place to start. Your decision will be influenced by how much desk space you have, and how comfortable you are while using the display. Some people think that a big screen is best, but then when they start to use it daily, they find that it’s too big. And the same goes for customers who think a small screen is best.

If you’re looking for a size to start with for your own personal research, we recommend 24 inches—just like with Apple’s iMac. That seems like a good size for most people, and it’s easy to go up or down from that point. Most people tend to go between 24 and 27 inches for home use.

For professionals—graphics, video, audio, even spreadsheets—a large screen will help you be more productive. Think 27 inches and higher. You’ll be able to fit more elements on the screen and not waste your time scrolling.

If on-screen real estate is valuable to you, consider a multi-display setup. A smaller screen can be used for things like chat, email, web, and more, while the bigger screen is your main workspace. Or get screens of the same size and maximize the space.

Screen resolution

Screen resolution can go hand-in-hand with screen size. Screen resolution refers to the number of pixels used to create what you see on the screen. The higher the resolution, the more detail you can see. Larger displays tend to have more resolution options, as well as the ability to support higher resolutions.

Often, when you find two displays that are the same size but have a wide price difference, it’s mostly because of the screen resolution. Monitors with high resolutions are more expensive. For example, Apple’s $1,599 Studio Display is 27 inches, and it has a high screen resolution of 5120×2880 (5K resolution). On the other hand, LG sells the 27-inch 27UK650-W, but it’s a 3840×2160 (4K) resolution display for content creators, and it’s $350–lower resolution, but $1,249 cheaper. (There actually aren’t other 27-inch 5K monitors available, except for the $1,449 LG UltraFine 27MD5KL-B.)

So what screen resolution should you get? Here are some suggestions; these are guidelines that you can adjust based on your preferences.

  • For general purpose use, such as web browsing, email, media viewing, small photo and video projects and viewing: 1920×1080 or 2560×1440 (HD)
  • For more-involved content creation, productivity, and media viewing: 3840×2160 (4K)
  • For pro-level content creation, productivity, and media viewing: 4K or higher

Want to use an 8K monitor? Read How to connect an 8K display to your Mac.

Connecting a monitor to a Mac

How a monitor connects to a Mac can be confusing. The traditional HDMI and DisplayPort connectors used by many monitors are being replaced–or complemented–by USB-C and Thunderbolt ports. And though USB-C and Thunderbolt cables may look the same, there are actually some important technical differences between them, so it’s important to check which ports your new monitor uses and make sure you buy the correct cables and adapters.

Most recent Mac models have Thunderbolt ports, so if you buy a monitor that has HDMI or DisplayPort interfaces only, then you’ll need an adapter to connect to the Mac. This can get a bit confusing, but Apple does provide a list of the ports included on most recent Mac models so that you can figure out what you need.

Apple also provides a guide to HDMI and DisplayPort technology, which covers Mac models going right back to 2008, so that should provide all the info you need for all the Macs you use at home or at work. Less expensive monitors still tend to use HDMI and DisplayPort, and while it’s not too costly to buy adapters that will allow you to connect your Mac, we reckon it’s worth future-proofing your new monitor by getting one that includes at least one USB-C or Thunderbolt port.

If a display uses Thunderbolt to connect to the Mac, it may have additional USB-C or Thunderbolt ports so the display can act as a hub. In this case, If you have a device you want to connect to your Mac, you can connect it to one of the ports on the monitor, which is already connected to the Mac and probably in an easier location for access.

Look for a USB-C or Thunderbolt connection with power delivery (PD) that can charge your MacBook. A 65W PD will be enough for a MacBook Air or 14-inch MacBook Pro, but you’ll need at least 90W for a 15-inch or 16-inch Pro.

Read our article on how to connect a second screen to a Mac which explains everything you need to know about how to identify which ports you have, the adapters you will require, and how to set things up.

Ergonomics

If you’re going to spend a lot of time sitting at a desk looking at your lovely new display then you need to keep ergonomics in mind. The ability to tilt the angle of the monitor back and forth, swivel it around for easy viewing, and adjust the height of the monitor in order to avoid an aching back or neck.

Some monitors can pivot or rotate in either landscape or portrait mode.

As a rough guide, there is a point at about 2 to 3 inches from the top of the screen that should be at eye level. Obviously, eye level varies from one person to another, so it’s important that you can adjust the screen for your own personal comfort. You may also prefer a monitor that doesn’t suffer from glare, or you will be forever repositioning the monitor (or your head) to compensate for that.

Other considerations

There are other considerations you’ll want to make when shopping for a monitor. A lot of these come down to personal preference or what you need for the work you do. They include:

  • Color space (gamut): The number of colors a monitor can show. Professionals need specific color spaces.
  • Refresh rate: The frequency when a screen is refreshed. Higher rates produce smoother animations.
  • Webcam: Some displays have a built-in camera you can use for FaceTime and other video conferencing apps, or to record yourself.
  • Speakers: If you plan on frequently viewing or listening to media, a good set of speakers makes for a better experience.

How many monitors does my Mac allow?

The number of external displays you can hook up to your Mac, depends on its M-series processor. In short, any Pro or Max M1 to M5 processor supports at least two monitors, but base M1/M2/M3 and Neo MacBooks might be limited to just one. See below for the full list and also a link to our tutorial about how to get round the limitations.

• If your Mac has a base (non-Pro or non-Max) M1 or M2 chip, or is the MacBook Neo, it is limited to using just one external monitor unless you follow our DisplayLink workaround tutorial.

• If your Mac has a base (non-Pro or non-Max) M3 chip, it can only use two external monitors if its own lid is closed (so not showing its own screen) unless you follow our tips in the link above.

• If your Mac has a base M4/M5, M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro or Max chip, it is limited to using two external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.

• If your Mac has an M5 Pro chip, it is limited to using three external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.

• If your Mac has an M5 Max chip, it is limited to using four external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.

entry.title: Apple’s new MacBook Pro finally breaks the grid
entry.content:
Macworld

This has been a year of major change with Apple’s MacBook lineup. 2026 started with simple and limited choices, and it’s ending with a robust lineup that broadens the MacBook’s appeal.

When the year started, Apple offered the MacBook Air, the laptop for the general consumer, and the MacBook Pro, the choice for professionals with higher demands. Those laptop were effective in reaching a large part of the market, but it was missing laptops at the two ends of the market: the sub-$1,000 market where budget-conscious shoppers are at, and the ultra-luxury market where money is no object.

In March, Apple released the MacBook Neo, a $599 laptop (now $699) that instantly became a hit in the budget market. And on Wednesday, Apple went in the completely opposite direction with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, a laptop that’s the rich pro’s pro. You’ll pay top dollar for it–starts at $2,899 for a 14-inch model, and a maxxed-out 16-inch model tops out at $14,549. Regardless of how you configure it, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR has top-notch features at its base, and it’s not difficult to find people who are willing to pay for it.

When 2026 started, a top-of-the-line MacBook Pro cost $7,199. What does nearly twice as much get you now? An OLED touchscreen display, a better sound system, a new design that’s about a pound lighter, and, just so everyone knows you have one, a glowing Apple logo for the first time in 10 years.

What about the grid?

At the 1998 Macworld Expo, Steve Jobs addressed the need for Apple to simplify its overly complicated Mac lineup. He presented what’s been dubbed the product grid, made up of two product lines (desktop and laptop) and two customer markets (consumer and professional). It’s been attributed as the core of Apple’s success and a testament to its simplicity. The company doesn’t get bogged down in too many SKUs and customers can easily find their desired product.

But over recent years, Apple’s Mac market share has been somewhat flat. Any noticeable jump in sales during a quarter was offset by a downturn soon after. It’s been reported that Apple wants its Mac market share to grow, and to do so it has determined that it needs to be more aggressive towards the attracting the fringes of the PC laptop market.

So it broke the grid. Instead of two options appealing to most people Apple needed to offer products to persuade those sitting on the fence to get off it and buy a MacBook. Now, there’s an affordable gateway into the Mac and an ultra-luxury option, along with the usual in-between options. Choices, choices.

The grid served its purpose but is now insufficient for a company the size of Apple. It’s time to move off it. What’s different now is that the MacBook Neo, MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, and MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display are distinct products with obvious feature separation. It doesn’t have the quaint simplicity of Jobs’ quadrant, but by expanding the grid, Apple has set up the Mac for a different kind of success—one that fills every need and leaves no wallet unturned.

Batteries will lose efficiency over time so don’t expect a 2010-era MacBook battery to still possess the same power as it did when it was new or more than a 2026 model, even if it had an originally higher Wh rating.

As you can see from the above battery capacities, the MacBook Pro features higher capacity batteries than the MacBook Air, although not by a truly significant margin.

For example, the 13-inch M3 MacBook Air’s battery was rated at 52.6Wh, while the 13-inch M2 MacBook Pro had a 58.2Wh battery.

The larger the laptop, the higher wattage is the battery—as they generally require more power to run the larger, brighter screens. The Air features a Liquid Retina display with 500 nits brightness while the Pro has a superior 1,000-nit Liquid Retina XDR display. The latest pro PROLED XDR Display MacBooks can reach 2,000 nits.

The newer MacBooks with more efficient processors will also gain extra battery life by not stressing the batteries as hard to complete the same tasks.

Apple claims that the current 13-inch M5 MacBook Air (53.8Wh) boasts up to 18 hours Apple TV app movie playback. The 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro has a higher capacity 72.4Wh battery and can keep going for 24 hours on the movie playback. The 16-inch M5 Pro has the same 24-hour video playback claim despite its 100Wh battery but it has to run the larger screen.

Battery life depends on many factors, particularly which and how many applications you are running at one time.

For more information on the differences between Apple’s laptop models, read our feature MacBook Air vs Pro: Which Mac laptop is right for you.

When you want to charge the MacBook’s battery, make sure you use the appropriate charger. Check out our recommendations for the best USB-C charger for your MacBook.

entry.title: Should you buy a MacBook Pro now? M6, touchscreen and older models compared
entry.content:
Macworld

Apple has launched an M6 MacBook Pro alongside a new touchscreen MacBook Pro with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. If you’re buying your first MacBook Pro or replacing an older model, now is a good time to consider your options – although we recommend reading independent reviews before committing.

If you already own an M4 or M5 MacBook Pro that meets your needs, there’s little reason to upgrade unless the touchscreen model’s combination of OLED, touch and lower weight appeals to you.

Apple increased MacBook Pro prices by $300 to $500 in June 2026, so discounts and refurbished models remain worth considering. For the best value, compare the non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max models and any remaining discounted M5 stock with the new models. If your purchase isn’t urgent, it may also be worth holding out for Black Friday deals at the end of November.

The MacBook Pro is best suited to creative professionals, software developers, engineers and other power users who need sustained performance, a premium display, plenty of ports and high memory configurations. If your workload consists mainly of web browsing, office work, studying or light creative tasks, the MacBook Air is likely to offer better value at a much lower price.

In this guide, we’ll help you decide which MacBook Pro is right for you, explain the best times of year to buy, highlight today’s best deals, and consider whether a refurbished model or MacBook Air would be a better choice.

Should you buy a MacBook Pro now?

Now that Apple has announced its latest MacBook Pros, there’s no need to wait for the launch to see your options. The M6 and touchscreen models arrive on November 6. If you’re considering either, we recommend waiting for independent reviews. If you need a laptop immediately, an existing non-touch M5 Pro or M5 Max model could still be a sensible purchase.

Buy a MacBook Pro now if:

  • You’re upgrading from an Intel Mac: Apple is ending support for Intel Macs, so if you haven’t yet switched to Apple Silicon, now is a good time to do so. As Intel Macs reach the end of support, they’ll stop receiving security updates, leaving them vulnerable to newly discovered security flaws.
  • You need a new laptop: If your current Mac is broken, unreliable or slowing you down, there’s little reason to wait.
  • You edit video or create content: Whether you’re editing 4K video, working in Photoshop or Lightroom, producing music or creating 3D graphics, the MacBook Pro delivers the sustained performance creative professionals need.
  • You’re a software developer, engineer or AI professional: Compiling code, running virtual machines, working with AI models or processing large datasets is much faster on the MacBook Pro, particularly the M5 Pro and M5 Max models.
  • You need sustained performance: Unlike the fanless MacBook Air, the MacBook Pro uses active cooling to maintain peak performance during long exports, renders and other demanding workloads.
  • You need professional features: The MacBook Pro offers a Liquid Retina XDR or PROLED XDR display with ProMotion, HDMI, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe charging and higher memory and storage options than the MacBook Air.
  • You find an excellent deal: A discounted MacBook Pro can be a good buy if it meets your needs. Compare its memory, storage, display and processor with the new models before deciding whether the saving is worthwhile.

When shouldn’t you buy a MacBook Pro?

The MacBook Pro is an excellent laptop, but it isn’t the right choice for everyone. If you don’t need its extra performance or professional features, you’ll save money – and probably be just as happy – with a MacBook Air. There are also a few situations where it’s worth waiting rather than buying today.

Don’t buy a MacBook Pro now if:

  • You want a processor upgrade over M5 Pro or M5 Max: The touchscreen models retain the same chip options as their non-touch equivalents. The M6 Pro or M6 Max aren’t expected until 2027.
  • You’re looking for the best price: With new MacBook Pro M6 models now here, discounts on the discontinued MacBook Pro M5 could be more attractive. Black Friday may bring further savings.
  • You mainly use your laptop for everyday tasks: If your workload consists of web browsing, Microsoft Office, streaming, email, video calls or light photo editing, a MacBook Air offers excellent performance for much less money.
  • You’re a student with basic computing needs: If your coursework mainly involves writing essays, researching online or creating presentations, a MacBook Air is likely to be the better value.
  • Portability is your priority: The MacBook Air is thinner, lighter and completely silent thanks to its fanless design, although the touchscreen MacBook Pro is lighter than its non-touchscreen counterpart.
  • You’re on a budget: The MacBook Air delivers outstanding performance for most users while costing significantly less than the MacBook Pro.

For most people, the MacBook Air is the better buy. The MacBook Pro only comes into its own if you regularly run demanding professional workloads that benefit from its active cooling, more powerful chips, superior display, additional ports and higher memory options.

Should I buy a MacBook Pro: At a glance

MacBook Pro: Current line up

Apple’s MacBook Pro range now offers three main choices: the entry-level 14-inch M6, the non-touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max models, and the new M5 Pro and M5 Max models with PROLED XDR touchscreen displays. Retailers may also have remaining stock of the previous entry-level M5 MacBook Pro.

MacBook Pro M6

Introduced in October 2026, the 14-inch M6 is the entry-level MacBook Pro. It starts with a 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, 16GB of unified memory and 1TB of storage. It retains the previous model’s design and non-touch Liquid Retina XDR display, while adding the M6 processor, Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Choose it if you want the Pro’s display, ports and active cooling without paying for an M5 Pro or M5 Max configuration. From $1,999/£1,999.

Launched in March 2026, these models introduced Apple’s Fusion Architecture, combining two 3nm dies into a single system-on-chip. They offer:

  • M5 Pro: up to 18-core CPU (6 super cores, 12 performance cores).
  • M5 Max: up to 40-core GPU, up to 128GB RAM, and up to 8TB storage.
  • Thunderbolt 5, Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 6 via Apple’s N1 wireless chip.

It doesn’t buy a newer processor generation. Equivalent models retain the same M5 Pro or M5 Max chip options and Apple’s advertised battery-life ratings. Think of this primarily as a display and portability upgrade.

The extra cost may be worthwhile if you spend much of your working day using the built-in screen, particularly for visual work, or regularly carry your laptop between locations. If your MacBook spends most of its time connected to an external monitor, the non-touch version is likely to offer better value.

  • Buyers working directly on photographs, video or other visual content may value the package more.
  • Read reviews that include testing of touch ergonomics, reflections, fingerprints and app support before buying.

What’s the best MacBook Pro price right now?

Foundry

Apple rarely discounts Macs itself. In fact, in June 2026, Apple increased MacBook Pro prices by $300 to $500, making it more important than ever to shop around for a deal.

The price rise came in the middle of Amazon’s Prime Day sale, when the M5 MacBook Pro briefly hit record-low prices. Discounts brought the entry-level model down to $1,499/£1,529, making it one of the best MacBook Pro deals we’ve ever tracked. When is the best time to buy a MacBook Pro?

Foundry

If you’re looking for the lowest price on a MacBook Pro, the best times to buy are during major sales events such as Amazon Prime Day in June/July or October and Black Friday.

Black Friday is typically the strongest shopping period for MacBook Pro deals, although the lowest prices are often reserved for older or clearance models, and popular configurations can sell out quickly. We expect the Black Friday 2026 deals to start towards the beginning of November.

Another time to look for deals is shortly after Apple launches a new model, as retailers often discount the previous generation to clear remaining stock, making it possible to save hundreds if you don’t need the latest chip.

If you’re a student, you can save all year. Students, teachers, and education staff can typically save $100 to $200 on a new MacBook Pro through Apple’s Education Store. However, the best time to buy is usually during Apple’s annual Back to School promotion in the summer, when qualifying customers can often claim a free pair of AirPods or another bonus gift alongside the education discount. See How to use Apple’s Education Store to get a bargain.

Is buying a refurbished MacBook Pro a good idea?

Foundry

Buying a refurbished MacBook Pro can be a great way to save money – particularly if you buy directly from Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store.

Apple Certified Refurbished Macs are typically around 15% cheaper than brand-new models and come with the same one-year warranty, 90 days of complimentary technical support, and the option to purchase AppleCare+. Every Mac undergoes extensive testing, is cleaned and inspected, and receives genuine Apple replacement parts where necessary.

The main downside is availability. Stock changes daily, so you may need to wait for the exact model, storage capacity, memory configuration, or colour you want. Newer MacBook Pro models also usually don’t appear in the refurbished store until several months after launch.

Third-party retailers, including Amazon, also sell refurbished Macs, but quality standards vary considerably. We generally recommend avoiding Macs that are more than five years old, as they may receive fewer years of macOS and security updates. In some cases, retailers also offer larger discounts on new, previous-generation MacBook Pro models during major sales events, so it’s always worth comparing prices before you buy.

For most buyers, Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store remains the safest and best-value way to buy a refurbished MacBook Pro.

Which MacBook Pro to choose

Choose the M6 MacBook Pro if you want Pro features such as the better display, extra ports and active cooling, but don’t need the power of the M5 Pro or M5 Max.

Choose the M5 Pro MacBook Pro if you’re a professional who regularly edits 4K video, compiles large software projects, works with RAW photos, produces music or runs multiple demanding applications at once. For most creative professionals and developers, the M5 Pro offers the best balance of performance and price.

Choose the M5 Max MacBook Pro if your work pushes a laptop to its limits. The M5 Max is designed for users editing multiple streams of 8K video, creating complex 3D animations, running large AI or machine learning workloads, or handling visual effects and other GPU-intensive tasks. Unless you regularly perform these types of work, the M5 Pro is likely to offer better value.

Choose an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display if its OLED touchscreen and lighter design justify the extra $400/£400. Choose between Pro and Max according to your workload; you don’t need the Max chip to get the new display.

What about the MacBook Air?

Stephan Wiesend

If you’re considering a MacBook Pro, it’s also worth looking at the MacBook Air. Apple updated the Air in March 2026, and with a starting price of $1,299/£1,299 (the price increased by $200/£200 in June 2026), it’s significantly cheaper than the MacBook Pro.

The MacBook Air is a good choice if you:

  • Mainly browse the web, use Microsoft Office or stream media.
  • Are a student or home user with light computing needs.
  • Value portability and a silent, fanless design.
  • Want the best value MacBook.

However, the lower price comes with a few compromises. Compared to the MacBook Pro, the Air offers lower sustained performance, a less advanced display, fewer ports, and lower memory and storage limits.

Choose the MacBook Pro if you need:

  • Sustained performance for video editing, coding, 3D rendering or AI workloads.
  • A Liquid Retina XDR display with ProMotion and HDR.
  • More connectivity, including HDMI, an SDXC card slot and additional Thunderbolt ports.
  • Higher-end M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, with up to 128GB of unified memory.

For most everyday users, the MacBook Air is the better value. But if your work regularly pushes your laptop to its limits, the MacBook Pro is well worth the extra investment.

Do you need to upgrade your current Mac?

Apple

Whether you need to upgrade depends on three things: how old your Mac is, whether Apple still supports it, and whether it can keep up with the apps and features you use every day.

If you have an Intel Mac, it’s time to upgrade

With macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple has ended support for Intel Macs. While Apple is expected to continue providing security updates for the small number of Intel Macs that support macOS 26 Tahoe, that support is likely to last only another year or two.

The only Intel Macs that can run macOS Tahoe are:

  • 16-inch MacBook Pro (2019)
  • 13-inch MacBook Pro (2020, four Thunderbolt ports)
  • 27-inch iMac (2020)
  • Mac Pro (2019)

If your Mac isn’t on this list, it may no longer receive the latest macOS updates and will eventually stop receiving security updates. For more advice, read How long Macs and MacBooks last: Lifespan, support and when to upgrade.

If you’re still using an Intel Mac, we recommend upgrading as soon as your budget allows. Moving from Intel to Apple Silicon is one of the biggest upgrades Apple has ever offered. You’ll benefit from dramatically faster performance, much longer battery life, quieter operation, Apple Intelligence support, and many more years of macOS compatibility. Read our guides to macOS Tahoe and macOS Golden Gate to see what you’ll gain by upgrading.

Which are the best retailers to buy a MacBook from?

Aside from Apple (View the MacBook Pro in the Apple Store and View the MacBook Pro in the Apple Store U.K). There are a number of third-party resellers that frequently discount the MacBook Pro.

When shopping at a reseller our advice is to always verify:

entry.title: Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display: 5 top features
entry.content:
Macworld

Apple on Wednesday announced the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, a new luxury addition to the high end of its MacBook lineup. Available in 14- and 16-inch models, the base price starts at $2,899/£2,899 and $3,399/£3,399, respectively. That’s $400 more than the comparable non-OLED models.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display reimagines the MacBook Pro with several features that appeal to the most demanding users. Here are the top features of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

Touchscreen input

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is Apple’s first touchscreen Mac. Now, users can tap on the screen in addition to typing on the keyboard and using the built-in trackpad. The touchscreen is in addition to these traditional input methods; it doesn’t replace them.

Users can use touch gestures that are familiar: scrolling can be done with swiping, pinch to zoom, double-tap a window to fill the screen, and more. Apple built the touch sensor directly into the display panel so latency is minimized.

Apple

The key to a successful touchscreen experience is accommodating software, and Apple has made several touch enhancements throughout macOS 27 Golden Gate. For example, Safari tabs “lift” and then enlarge as you drag it to a new location, then go back to their original size when dropped, and buttons enlarge when it sense your fingers on the screen.  Apple has also made system gesture APIs available so developers can configure their software for touch.

OLED display

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is also the first MacBook to feature a tandem OLED display.  Two OLED panels are stacked together to provide an overall improved screen experience. Apple first introduced tandem OLEDs in the 2024 iPad Pro.

Marketed by Apple as a PROLED XDR display, tandem OLEDs produce deeper blacks, more contrast, and better colors. Apple rates the XDR brightness at 1,000 nits sustained full-screen, 2,000 nits peak for HDR content only, and an SDR brightness up to 1,000 nits sustained full-screen, 2,000 nits peak. That’s a big improvement over the mini-LED models.

Apple

Apple calls the display a “portable reference monitor,” a statement targeted at professionals who demand color accuracy. The laptop’s display engine controls color and luminance at the sub-millisecond level for content, pixel use, temperature, and environment. With support for ProMotion, the display supports variable refresh rates up to 120Hz. The new genlock feature syncs the display’s refresh rate with a connected camera’s capture rate.

Apple has also made structural improvements for touch input. A new hinge will provide better stability, and video stabilization is used to smooth the camera feed when using touch on a video call.

Dynamic Island

The new pill-shaped Dynamic Island is on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, replacing the notch on the MacBook Pro. It acts just like it does on the iPhone, serving as a central area for Live Activities, notifications, controls, and other UI elements.

Apple

On the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, the Dynamic Island is the anchor point for Spotlight and Siri AI. When activating those features, the text window for user input opens under the pill box.

Thinner and lighter design

Apple has made the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display smaller than its MacBook Pro counterparts. At 3 pounds (1.4 kg), the 14-inch model is a half-pound (.2 kg)  lighter; the 16-inch model weighs 4 pounds (1.82 kg) and is .6 pounds (.31 kg) lighter.

Here are how the dimensions compare.

The design also features the triumphant return of the glowing Apple logo on the lid. Introduced on the PowerBook G3 in 1999, the glowing Apple was replaced when Apple introduced the 12-inch MacBook in 2015. In 2016, Apple replaced it on the MacBook Pro.

M5 Pro and M5 Max chips

Like the MacBook Pro (which are not replaced by the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display and remains in Apple’s lineup), the new laptop comes with either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip.

The M5 Max is Apple’s fastest chip in a laptop, beating the previous fastest laptop chip, the M4 Max, by about 12 percent in multi-core CPU and 7 percent in single-core CPU Geekbench 7 tests. Apple current fastest chip overall is the M5 Ultra, but its cooling requirements restrict it to the desktop Mac Studio.

  • 18-core CPU, 40-core GPU starts with 48GB of RAM, upgradeable to 64GB or 128GB

Other new features

The  MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also features:

  • A six-speaker audio system with a new woofer design for added bass.
  • Audio tuning for closed-lid use when connected to an external display.
  • Advanced video stabilization in the camera
  • Up to 16TB of SSD storage.

Prices

Here are the starting prices for the  MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. They all cost $400 more than the equivalent non-OLED mdoels.

entry.title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro Guide: Release date, price and new features
entry.content:
Macworld

Apple has announced its first touchscreen MacBook Pro lineup, officially called MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Available in 14.2-inch and 16.3-inch sizes with M5 Pro or M5 Max processors, the new models combine tandem OLED technology with direct touchscreen input. Touch is standard across the new range, while non-touchscreen MacBook Pros remain available.

The biggest changes include Dynamic Island, a smaller and lighter enclosure, and a new 16TB maximum SSD option on M5 Max configurations. The display adds Adobe RGB support and higher peak brightness while retaining a maximum 120Hz refresh rate. Other features include up to 128GB of RAM, Thunderbolt 5, Wi-Fi 7 and audio with a claimed 50% deeper bass.

The touchscreen models retain the same chip families, memory capacities and advertised battery endurance as their equivalent non-touch M5 models, making this primarily an upgrade to the display, design and how users interact with their Mac. U.S. starting prices carry a $400 premium over equivalent non-touch versions, with the 14-inch M5 Pro starting at $2,899 and the 16-inch M5 Max starting at $4,799.

What’s new compared with the non-touchscreen MacBook Pro?

The processor generation, maximum RAM, Thunderbolt generation, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth versions and Apple’s battery-life ratings haven’t changed, but there is a lot that is different.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?

  • Pre-orders: October 28, 2026
  • On sale: November 6, 2026

Pre-orders opened on October 28, 2026, through Apple’s website and Apple Store app.

Deliveries and retail availability begin Friday, November 6, through Apple Stores and Apple Authorised Resellers. Apple announces an initial rollout covering 30 countries and regions.

Pre-order the touchscreen MacBook Pro PROLED XDR from Apple U.S.

Pre-order the touchscreen MacBook Pro PROLED XDR from Apple U.K.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro price

Apple has introduced a more expensive touchscreen range alongside the existing models. The new range carries a $400 starting-price premium over every equivalent non-touch M5 model. The premium does not buy a newer processor generation, more base memory or a larger entry SSD.

Apple 14-inch MacBook Pro PROLED XDR (M5 Pro, 2026)

Price When Reviewed: $2,899
Best Prices Today: $2899 at Apple

Touchscreen MacBook Pro design

Apple

The new MacBook Pro retains a conventional laptop layout, built-in keyboard and Force Touch trackpad. It comes in Space Black or Silver, with an enclosure made from 100% recycled aluminium.

Compared to the existing models, the weight reduction is more substantial than the thickness reduction: the 14-inch models lose 220g, while the 16-inch models lose approximately 310–320g. Slimmer borders also allow the larger screen to grow slightly despite a reduced enclosure footprint.

Apple describes a revised hinge and cooling system. It claims greater hinge stability during touch input and says the cooling design directs warm air away from the display. We’ll be verifying those claims in our review of the new laptop.

Touchscreen MacBook display

Apple

Both sizes offer M5 Pro and M5 Max configurations, and every PROLED XDR model includes touch. There is no base-M6 configuration in this touchscreen range.

OLED’s benefits concern image reproduction: individually lit pixels, deeper blacks and reduced blooming around bright objects. Touch adds a separate benefit – direct interaction with content. The maximum refresh rate remains 120Hz.

Apple indicates that pixel compensation mitigates ageing and burn-in, rather than establishing that OLED cannot deteriorate. It quotes 1% reflectance for standard glass; nano-texture scatters reflections further.

There is also an oleophobic coating to reduce fingerprints. For cleaning, Apple advises powering down and using a soft cloth appropriately dampened for standard screens; never spray liquid directly onto the display. For nano-texture, use the supplied polishing cloth and follow Apple’s specific care instructions.

Which MacBook models get a touchscreen?

Touch comes with the 14- and 16-inch PROLED XDR models using M5 Pro or M5 Max; the M6 MacBook Pro and Liquid Retina XDR models have no touchscreen.

How does touch work in macOS?

Apple

Apple confirms scrolling, pinch-to-zoom, drawing, dragging and dropping, double-tapping a window to fill the screen, and flicking windows into tiled positions. Touch works alongside keyboard and trackpad input.

Dynamic Island provides access to activities and controls. Spotlight’s relocation there requires Siri AI to be available and enabled.

In everyday use, this offers a direct way to move through documents, enlarge photographs or reposition content.

macOS translates taps into clicks for many existing apps; developers can use gesture APIs for more specialised controls.

Apple indicated that there are forthcoming updates for Microsoft 365, Notion, Canva, Zoom, Lightroom, DaVinci Resolve, Blender, Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Shapr3D and djay Pro later this year. Creator Studio updates are confirmed to be coming in November.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro processor

  • M5 Pro and M5 Max

As expected, the processors are carried-over M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. The new models feature the same CPU/GPU options, Neural Engine and memory bandwidth as the equivalent non-touch models.

All have a 16-core Neural Engine and GPU Neural Accelerators. The 18-core CPU comprises six “super cores” and 12 performance cores; the 15-core version has five and 10 respectively.

Apple introduced these chips earlier in 2026. They use third-generation 3nm manufacturing and Apple’s Fusion Architecture, joining two dies into one system-on-chip through advanced packaging. Those are characteristics of the existing M5 Pro/Max generation, not manufacturing upgrades introduced with touch.

For an example of Apple’s older-generation comparisons, it claims 10.9× faster time to first token than M1 Pro for a 14-inch M5 Pro model. Apple’s test used an 18-core CPU/20-core GPU, 64GB RAM and 4TB SSD against an M1 Pro with 10-core CPU/16-core GPU, 32GB RAM and 8TB SSD. The workload was a quantised 14-billion-parameter model, an 8K-token prompt and LM Studio.

Apple made no indication that there was any CPU/GPU performance increase over an equivalent non-touch M5 configuration, or a quantified improvement in whole-system power efficiency.

Separately, Apple has launched the 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip.

Touchscreen MacBook memory: How much RAM is included?

There is no increase in base or maximum memory over the equivalent non-touch M5 models. The M5 Pro starts with 24GB, the 32-core GPU M5 Max has 36GB, and the 40-core version starts with 48GB.

Reaching 64GB with M5 Pro requires the 20-core GPU; reaching 128GB requires the 40-core M5 Max.

More memory can accommodate larger creative projects, more demanding multitasking and larger local AI models.

Touchscreen MacBook storage: What is the highest capacity?

The entry capacities are unchanged. However, it is possible to upgrade to 16TB on M5 Max, up from 8TB. In order to obtain that capacity buyers need either the 32-core or 40-core GPU.

Apple makes an “up to twice as fast” storage claim that compares a 16TB M5 Max system with an 8TB M4 Max system. Both had 128GB RAM; testing used FIO 3.43 with 1,024KB requests, a 10GB file and queue depth eight. That test doesn’t demonstrate doubled SSD performance over the non-touch M5 range. We will be running our own benchmarks.

Touchscreen MacBook camera, microphones and speakers

The camera remains a 12MP Center Stage camera with Desk View and 1080p video recording. Advanced video stabilisation is new, however.

Authentication remains Touch ID. Dynamic Island is an interface feature, not confirmation of Face ID or a TrueDepth camera.

Apple retains a six-speaker system, force-cancelling woofers, Spatial Audio and Dolby Atmos support. Apple claims 50% deeper bass and adds closed-lid audio tuning.

The three-microphone array retains directional beamforming, Voice Isolation and Wide Spectrum modes.

Touchscreen MacBook battery

Apple lists video-streaming ratings of 22/20 hours for the 14-inch Pro/Max and 24/22 hours for the 16-inch Pro/Max, the same as the non-touchscreen models.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro connectivity and ports

Both sizes include:

  • One 3.5mm headphone jack with support for high-impedance headphones.
  • Three Thunderbolt 5 USB-C ports, supporting charging and DisplayPort.
  • One HDMI port.
  • One SDXC card slot.
  • MagSafe 3.

Apple quotes Thunderbolt/USB4 support up to 120Gb/s and DisplayPort 2.1.

Apple’s N1 wireless chip, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread are included, but they are not touchscreen-model upgrades.

External display support

The M5 Pro chip supports three external displays at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz. Alternatively, it can support one 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz display, plus a second at up to 5K/120Hz or 4K/200Hz.

The M5 Max chip supports four external displays at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz, or two displays at up to 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz.

Apple’s PROLED XDR specifications lists 165Hz for the multi-display 4K configurations, rather than the older 144Hz figure.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro versus non-touchscreen specs

Should you buy the touchscreen MacBook Pro?

Is touch worth the premium? Provisionally, the stronger justification is the combined OLED display, lower weight and touch capability. Buyers who regularly manipulate visual content may find direct input useful. Those who mainly type, use a mouse or work on an external display have less reason to pay the extra $400. A firm verdict needs testing of reflections, fingerprints, reach, hinge movement and app behaviour.

Which model? The 14-inch M5 Pro is the most accessible and portable option. Choose the 16-inch M5 Pro for a larger workspace and Apple’s longest battery rating. M5 Max makes sense when GPU performance, memory bandwidth, more than 64GB RAM or storage above 4TB serves a demonstrated workload; it is unnecessary simply to obtain touch.

Should existing owners upgrade? For owners of an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro, this is principally a screen and portability decision. M4 owners should similarly assess the display benefits against the cost. Older Apple-silicon and Intel owners may gain more broadly, but performance improvements vary by application.

This or an iPad Pro? Choose the MacBook Pro when desktop Mac applications, its keyboard, ports and professional workflows are essential. Choose an iPad Pro when a handheld tablet and supported Apple Pencil workflow are central. Apple has not established Pencil support, a detachable display or tablet conversion for this MacBook Pro.
